Trying to Conceive

Sperm DNA and recurrent pregnancy loss: making sense of the tests

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After repeated pregnancy losses, it is reasonable to ask whether sperm could be part of the explanation. That question deserves a shared assessment rather than blame. A sperm count, a chromosome test and a sperm DNA fragmentation test examine different things. Understanding those differences can help you discuss which investigations might be useful and what a result could realistically change.

Include both partners in the assessment

Pregnancy loss is not automatically a problem with the person who carried the pregnancy. The embryo receives genetic material from both the egg and sperm, and several maternal, paternal and embryonic factors can matter. Sometimes investigations do not identify a clear explanation. Neither an unexplained loss nor an abnormal sperm result establishes that someone caused the loss through something they did.

Ask about a recurrent-loss assessment after repeated miscarriages rather than waiting for a general infertility timeline. Definitions and referral pathways differ: ASRM’s 2026 guidance uses two or more pregnancy losses, while RCOG describes recurrent miscarriage as three or more early losses. Your history may justify earlier investigation. Bring records of previous pregnancies and test results, including any testing of pregnancy tissue, and ask how both partners will be included.

Separate three different laboratory questions

A routine semen analysis describes features such as sperm number, movement and shape. It is useful in a fertility assessment, but it does not directly measure all damage within sperm DNA. A reassuring routine report therefore does not answer every question about repeated loss; an abnormal report also does not prove why a pregnancy ended.

A sperm DNA fragmentation test assesses damage to DNA in a sperm sample. A parental karyotype, usually obtained from a blood sample, examines the number and structure of chromosomes in the parent’s cells. Testing pregnancy tissue examines that pregnancy. These tests are not interchangeable. Before agreeing to a “genetic test,” ask whose cells will be tested and precisely which question the test can address.

Chromosome rearrangements are different from DNA fragmentation

Chromosomes are packages of genetic material. Most body cells usually have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, with one member of each pair inherited from each parent. A karyotype can identify some changes in chromosome number or structure. It cannot identify every possible genetic change, and a normal result does not guarantee that a future pregnancy will develop normally.

A balanced translocation is a rearrangement in which chromosome material has moved but none has been gained or lost. A carrier may have no related health problems, yet a pregnancy can inherit an unbalanced arrangement with extra or missing material. Either partner can carry a rearrangement. Its implications depend on the actual finding, so ask for genetic counselling instead of interpreting a chromosome diagram or risk percentage alone.

What sperm DNA fragmentation means

Fragmentation refers to breaks in sperm DNA. Laboratory methods include TUNEL, the comet assay, the sperm chromatin structure assay and the sperm chromatin dispersion test. They assess DNA damage in different ways. A percentage or index should be interpreted with the method and laboratory’s validated reference information; numbers from different tests should not be treated as directly interchangeable.

DNA damage is not the same as an inherited chromosome rearrangement, low sperm count or dead sperm. Some sperm DNA damage may be repaired by the egg after fertilisation. Higher damage has been associated with poorer reproductive outcomes, but it does not mean that conception is impossible or that every pregnancy will miscarry. A result cannot retrospectively identify which sperm fertilised a particular egg or, by itself, establish the cause of that loss.

Association does not provide an individual prediction

Studies comparing groups have often found higher DNA fragmentation among partners of people with recurrent pregnancy loss, but the findings are not uniform. Definitions of recurrent loss, laboratory methods and comparison groups vary. A group-level association is useful for research and discussion; it is not a personal miscarriage probability or proof that correcting a laboratory score will prevent another loss.

A study published in 2025 compared 634 men from couples with recurrent loss with 851 men without recurrent loss who were undergoing fertility evaluation. It found no statistically significant difference in DNA fragmentation or routine semen measures between the groups. This observational comparison neither proves that sperm DNA never matters nor tests a treatment. It illustrates why a single study should not become a diagnosis or a guarantee.

Why clinicians may give different advice about testing

Guidelines differ in how they translate the evidence into practice. The AUA/ASRM male-infertility guideline, amended in 2024, recommends evaluating the male partner in recurrent-loss couples with a karyotype and DNA fragmentation testing. It also advises against DNA fragmentation testing as part of every initial infertility assessment. The ESHRE recurrent-loss update of 2022 says fragmentation testing could be considered for diagnostic purposes.

ASRM’s 2026 recurrent-loss opinion says testing may be considered in otherwise unexplained recurrent miscarriage or when infertility is also present. RCOG’s 2023 patient information explains that sperm DNA testing is not usually offered because it is unclear whether treatment improves the chance of a healthy pregnancy. These are different recommendations, not evidence that every couple must buy a test or that no couple could benefit from discussing one. Ask which guidance applies to your situation.

Discuss the decision before paying for a test

Ask what would happen after a high result, a low result or an uncertain result. Would it lead to a reproductive-urology appointment, investigation of a specific condition, or a different treatment recommendation? If the proposed plan would be identical whatever the answer, ask what the test adds. The ESHRE guidance also acknowledges that the most informative and reliable fragmentation assay has not been established.

If testing is chosen, request the laboratory’s collection instructions and tell the team about recent illness, medicines and any collection difficulty. Discuss whether a repeat is needed and what question it would answer. Keep copies of the method, result and interpretation. A label such as “high fragmentation” is not a complete treatment plan, and a fall in that number should not be presented as proof of improved live-birth chances.

If a parental chromosome change is found

Referral for genetic counselling can clarify the specific rearrangement, possible pregnancy outcomes and available choices. Parental testing is selected differently across guidelines; the 2026 ASRM opinion supports offering it when pregnancy-tissue testing finds an unbalanced structural rearrangement or when chromosome testing of miscarriages is unavailable. Ask how your tissue results and family history affect the recommendation.

Some couples consider another unassisted pregnancy; others discuss IVF with preimplantation genetic testing for structural rearrangements, called PGT-SR, or donor eggs or sperm. PGT-SR is not a test for sperm DNA fragmentation and does not repair chromosomes. It may help select embryos for transfer, but evidence has not established its overall advantage over trying without IVF for every carrier couple. Discuss likely usable embryos, costs, time, limitations and your preferences.

Address identified problems without promising a cure

A reproductive specialist may review smoking, significant heat or chemical exposures, recent fever, medicines, infection symptoms, age and conditions such as a varicocele. Several of these are associated with sperm DNA damage. Evaluation should identify relevant problems rather than assume that one habit caused previous losses. Bring prescribed medicines, nonprescription products and supplements to the discussion; make medication changes with the responsible clinician.

Support for smoking cessation, balanced everyday habits and management of an identified condition can be worthwhile. However, an intervention that improves a sperm measure is not automatically a proven treatment for recurrent miscarriage. Do not let a supplement advertisement replace assessment or interpret unsuccessful treatment as a personal failure. Agree on realistic goals and review timing, taking both partners’ circumstances into account.

Be precise about ICSI, sperm selection and surgery

ICSI injects a selected sperm into an egg during IVF; it is not a general repair procedure for damaged DNA. Surgical retrieval may yield sperm with less measured fragmentation in selected cases, but it is invasive and the evidence has limitations. EAU guidance considers testicular sperm use for high fragmentation experimental. A high test result alone should not be presented as an automatic reason for surgery.

PICSI is an additional selection step based on sperm binding to hyaluronic acid. In the 2019 HABSelect randomised trial, it did not significantly improve the main outcome of full-term live birth compared with standard ICSI. There were fewer miscarriages, a secondary outcome, but this was not a trial specifically of couples with recurrent loss. HFEA advises discussing these limitations and the continuing risks of ICSI. Ask about evidence for your group, alternatives and additional costs rather than accepting a promised “best sperm” solution.

Make a follow-up plan that leaves room for uncertainty

At the next appointment, agree which results are being interpreted together, who coordinates care and when you will review the plan. A normal result cannot promise a baby, and an abnormal result does not mean there is no hope. Prognosis depends on the wider pregnancy history and clinical findings. Avoid applying a general success percentage to your family without that context. Both partners can ask for counselling or support while deciding what comes next.

Current pregnancy symptoms need their own assessment. Seek urgent medical help for spotting, light bleeding, unusual vaginal discharge or fluid leakage in pregnancy. If vaginal bleeding is accompanied by severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, seek emergency help; heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after putting it on also needs emergency help. Do not wait for a sperm test or a recurrent-loss appointment to address these symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret the full reproductive history and both partners’ findings together. Chromosome testing, semen analysis and sperm DNA testing address different questions.

AUA/ASRM, ASRM recurrent-loss guidance, ESHRE and RCOG differ on when to offer sperm DNA testing. Discuss the relevant guideline and how a result would change care.

Observational associations and changes in laboratory scores do not establish treatment benefit. Ask about live-birth outcomes, study populations and uncertainty before choosing additional procedures.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare a focused discussion about sperm DNA and chromosome questions after repeated loss. Keep copies of your results and ask for an agreed interpretation, appropriate referral and support for both partners.

When to seek help

Do not self-prescribe fertility treatment or change medicines without advice. Obtain urgent assessment for pregnancy spotting, light bleeding, unusual discharge or fluid leakage. Bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or collapse, or heavy bleeding soaking a pad quickly, needs emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sperm factors deserve consideration within a shared recurrent-loss assessment, without assigning blame.
  • Routine semen analysis, sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping answer different questions.
  • Guidelines differ about DNA fragmentation testing; ask what the result would change for you.
  • A better laboratory score is not proof that a treatment prevents miscarriage or guarantees a baby.
  • Genetic counselling, a written follow-up plan and emotional support can help you make informed choices.

Frequently asked questions

Can sperm contribute to miscarriage?

Paternal chromosome changes or sperm DNA damage can be relevant, but a loss cannot be attributed to sperm from a routine report alone. Both partners and the pregnancy history need consideration, and sometimes the explanation remains uncertain.

What is sperm DNA fragmentation, and does it always cause loss?

It means breaks in sperm DNA, assessed with specialist laboratory methods. Increased fragmentation has been associated with pregnancy loss, but it does not make infertility or miscarriage inevitable and is not a personal prediction.

Can lifestyle affect sperm DNA?

Smoking and some other exposures or health conditions are associated with DNA damage. Appropriate health support is sensible, but identifying a possible contributor does not prove that it caused a previous loss, and changing a habit cannot guarantee the next outcome.

Why assess the sperm-producing partner after repeated losses?

The assessment can identify relevant health or chromosome findings and help both partners understand their options. It is part of shared care, not an attempt to find someone to blame or a reason to ignore other causes.

Does a normal semen analysis rule out DNA damage?

No. Count, movement and shape do not directly answer every DNA question. A normal routine report does not prove fragmentation testing is needed either; discuss the history, guideline differences and likely effect on decisions.

Should everyone with a miscarriage buy a fragmentation test?

No. Recommendations concern selected circumstances, including recurrent loss, and differ between guidelines. Ask whether a test is appropriate for your history, which method is used and what would change after the result.

Is karyotyping the same as testing sperm DNA fragmentation?

No. A parental karyotype examines chromosome number and structure, usually in blood cells. Fragmentation testing assesses DNA damage in a sperm sample. A result from one cannot be substituted for the other.

Can IVF, PICSI or testicular sperm guarantee success?

No. These approaches have different indications, limits, costs and risks. Evidence from a selected fertility-treatment group does not automatically show benefit for recurrent loss, and no sperm-selection method guarantees a healthy live birth.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
